title: Data Visualization Market
note: The opening chapter cites this industry report to motivate the growing use of interactive charts and dashboards.

title: Trio: A System for Data, Uncertainty, and Lineage
authors: Parag Agrawal, Omar Benjelloun, Anish Das Sarma, Chris Hayworth, Shubha Nabar, Tomoe Sugihara, Jennifer Widom
note: Trio lets a query carry possible values and the evidence for each one. The thesis introduces it as an example of capturing lineage while evaluating SQL.
annotation: The thesis prints “An Introduction to ULDBs and the Trio System” here and at [9]. The linked VLDB demonstration matches the seven authors listed for [2].

title: GProM – A Swiss Army Knife for Your Provenance Needs
authors: Bahareh Arab, Su Feng, Boris Glavic, Seokki Lee, Xing Niu, Qitian Zeng
note: GProM translates requests for provenance into queries that run on an underlying database. The thesis places this middleware approach alongside approaches that instrument physical operators.

title: Column-Stores vs. Row-Stores: How Different Are They Really?
authors: Daniel J. Abadi, Samuel R. Madden, Nabil Hachem
note: A column store can defer reconstructing rows until an operator needs them. This helps explain why DuckDB’s selection vectors are useful when recording which input rows survive a filter.

title: Provenance for Interactive Visualizations
venue: HILDA · Workshop on Human-In-the-Loop Data Analytics
note: When someone selects a mark in a chart, a lineage query can identify the records behind it. That interaction supplies the latency motivation for the thesis.

title: Perm: Processing Provenance and Data on the Same Data Model through Query Rewriting
note: Perm rewrites relational queries so their results carry provenance. It provides a point of comparison for the thesis design, which captures relationships inside DuckDB operators.

title: Smoked Duck
note: Smoked Duck records row relationships as a vectorized query runs. My thesis built a physical scan and integrated lineage indexes so SQL could query those mappings.
annotation: The 2022 bibliography lists work in progress. SQLStepper, the related SIGMOD demonstration, appeared in 2023.

title: PUG: A Framework and Practical Implementation for Why and Why-Not Provenance
authors: Seokki Lee, Bertram Ludäscher, Boris Glavic
note: PUG explains both why a result exists and why an expected answer is missing. That second question extends the thesis’s central example of tracing an existing output row.

title: An Introduction to ULDBs and the Trio System
authors: Omar Benjelloun, Anish Das Sarma, Chris Hayworth, Jennifer Widom
venue: Stanford InfoLab · also in IEEE Data Engineering Bulletin
note: This introduction describes how Trio represents uncertain values and tracks their origins. It gives the data model behind the demonstration associated with reference [2].

title: Smoke: Fine-grained Lineage at Interactive Speed
note: Smoke captures relationships between rows during query execution so a later chart interaction can follow them quickly. Smoked Duck brings this idea to a vectorized execution engine.

title: DuckDB: an Embeddable Analytical Database
note: DuckDB runs analytical queries in the application process. Its vectorized operators, data chunks, and index joins form the execution environment that the thesis extends.

title: Provenance Semirings
authors: Todd J. Green, Grigoris Karvounarakis, Val Tannen
venue: PODS · Symposium on Principles of Database Systems
note: Semirings describe how annotations combine when a query has alternative or joint derivations. The thesis uses them to distinguish derivation polynomials from sets of contributing rows.

title: You Say ‘What’, I Hear ‘Where’ and ‘Why’: (Mis-)Interpreting SQL to Derive Fine-Grained Provenance
authors: Tobias Müller, Benjamin Dietrich, Torsten Grust
note: Reinterpreting a SQL query lets its operators compute dependencies at the level of individual cells. The thesis discusses this as a logical approach to capturing provenance.

title: Tracing the Lineage of View Data in a Warehousing Environment
authors: Yingwei Cui, Jennifer Widom, Janet L. Wiener
note: Given one item in a warehouse view, which source records produced it? This formulation anchors the thesis definition of lineage and the example of tracing an aggregate back to its inputs.
